title: Path models and regression with observed variables
summary: A path model is a structural model whose variables are all observed: each variable is one column drawn as a box, and a multiple regression is its simplest case.

body.text: Not every model needs latent variables. In [[path-analysis]] every variable is an [[observed-variable]]: one column of the data, such as a test score, a scale mean or a count. The arrows are regressions, estimated together as one system. A [[multiple-regression]] is the simplest path model: one outcome with arrows from several correlated predictors.

body.caption: A path model of observed variables (path-analysis notation: boxes, no ovals). Background predicts motivation, motivation predicts study hours, and three variables feed the exam score.

body.text: In a [[path-diagram]], **boxes are observed variables and ovals are latent variables**. In SEM Lab you build a path model by dragging data columns from the left pane onto empty canvas: each one becomes a box, and you draw the arrows between them. Technically each box is a construct with a single indicator. With nothing selected, the inspector can show every single-indicator construct as a box.

body.explanation: One regression equation per endogenous variable. Each β is a path coefficient, and ζ (the [[disturbance]]) is everything the equation leaves out. The model contains one such equation for Motivation, StudyHours and ExamScore each.

body.text: Both methods estimate the same equations. **CB-SEM (ML)** returns unstandardised coefficients in the variables' own units; in a recursive model they equal ordinary least squares, equation by equation. **PLS-SEM** returns standardised coefficients, because each construct score is just the standardised column, and R² is the regression R². Bootstrap intervals then give significance.

body.title: Fit is only testable when paths are left out
body.text: A regression, or any path model in which every possible arrow is present, is just-identified: [[degrees-of-freedom]] = 0, and χ², CFI and RMSEA show a perfect fit by construction. Only the arrows you deliberately leave out (here SES → StudyHours, PriorGPA → StudyHours and SES → ExamScore, so df = 3) can be tested.

items: Use a path model when each concept really is one measurement (age, hours, sales, a grade) or a well-validated scale score.
Use latent constructs when you have several items per concept: a single score is treated as free of [[measurement-error]], which attenuates the paths.
Dummy variables and interaction terms work only if you create them as columns in the data first.

mistake.title: Reading perfect fit of a just-identified model as support
mistake.text: A multiple regression drawn as a path model always fits perfectly in CB-SEM (df = 0, CFI = 1, RMSEA = 0). That says nothing about the theory. Report the coefficients and R² instead, and use fit only for models whose omitted paths make testable claims.

tryIt.task: Open the study-success example and run it (CB-SEM, ML). Check that df = 3, note which three paths are missing, then read the indirect effect of motivation on the exam score through study hours.

checks.question: You draw a multiple regression with four correlated predictors as a path model and estimate it with CB-SEM (ML). How many degrees of freedom does it have?

options.text: 0: the model is just-identified, so its fit is perfect by construction.
options.feedback: Correct. Every possible arrow is present, so the model reproduces the covariance matrix exactly.
Each predictor adds one free path, but its variance and covariances are free as well. Nothing is left over to test.

options.text: N − 5, as in the regression F test.
options.feedback: That is the residual df of OLS. SEM df counts covariance moments minus free parameters, and here they are equal.

checks.explanation: df = (number of variances and covariances) − (free parameters). A regression uses all of them, so df = 0. Fit becomes testable only when paths are left out.

checks.question: In a path diagram, how are observed and latent variables drawn?

options.text: Observed variables as boxes, latent variables as ovals.
options.feedback: Correct. This is the standard notation, and SEM Lab draws a path model's variables as boxes.

options.text: Observed variables as ovals, latent variables as boxes.
options.feedback: The other way round: a box is something you measured directly.

options.text: The shape is a matter of taste.
options.feedback: The shapes carry meaning: readers infer whether a variable is measured or inferred from them.

checks.explanation: Boxes (rectangles) are measured columns; ovals (circles) are latent variables, including disturbances.

checks.question: In PLS-SEM, every construct of a path model has exactly one indicator. What do the path coefficients equal?

options.text: The standardised OLS regression coefficients of each equation.
options.feedback: Correct. Each construct score is the standardised column, so PLS solves the same regressions on standardised data.
PLS works on standardised scores. The unstandardised slopes come from CB-SEM ML.
Only for a single predictor. With several correlated predictors the coefficients are partial effects.

checks.explanation: Single-indicator constructs make PLS-SEM an equation-by-equation regression on standardised variables; R² is the regression R².
